issues.legal_issue: A statutory allottee in possession of evacuee property has standing to challenge an order that threatens the allottee’s possessory rights.
material_facts: The occupants held the property under allotments made by the Custodian and were in possession when a claim seeking restoration of the property was allowed.
The order challenged by the occupants would have affected their continued possession, which could be ended only on grounds and by procedures specified in the governing law.
issues.conclusion: The allottees had a legal interest sufficient to challenge the adverse order in writ proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: Article 226 ordinarily requires an applicant to show an affected legal right. Statutory allottees have enforceable possessory interests even though those interests are not constitutional property rights; those interests are protected under the applicable statutory scheme. The Court relied on State of Punjab v. Suraj Prakash Kapur, which drew on Amar Singh v. Custodian, Evacuee Property, Punjab, and on Udit Narain Singh Malpaharia v. Additional Member Board of Revenue, Bihar & Anr., concerning parties affected by orders challenged through certiorari.

predicates.statutory_allottee_in_possession: The person challenging the order occupies the property under an allotment made by the statutory property administrator.
predicates.challenged_order_threatens_possession: The challenged order could displace the occupant or otherwise impair the occupant’s legally protected possession.

issues.definition: When a statutory allottee occupies property and the challenged order threatens that possession, the allottee may challenge the order.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory property administrator may challenge an order that impairs the administrator’s duty and authority to protect and manage evacuee property.
material_facts: The Custodian General and the Custodian filed a writ petition challenging the Tribunal’s order.
The order affected property administered by the Custodian and curtailed the Custodian’s powers.
The Tribunal was an independent statutory authority whose orders could not be corrected by another authority under the Act.
issues.conclusion: The Custodian General and the Custodian had standing to challenge the Tribunal’s order.
issues.legal_principle: The statutory scheme entrusted the Custodian not only with quasi-judicial functions but also with administration, management, and protection of evacuee property, including powers under Sections 9, 9A and 10. An administrator charged with protecting that property may challenge an order that adversely affects the property or the administrator’s statutory powers. The Court distinguished Md. Sharfuddin v. R.P. Singh & Ors. because the statutory scheme considered there was different.

predicates.statutory_property_administrator: The person challenging the order has statutory responsibility for administering and protecting the property at issue.
predicates.challenged_order_impairs_protection_duti: The challenged order adversely affects the property or restricts the administrator’s authority to protect or manage it.

issues.definition: When a statutory property administrator’s protection duties are impaired by an order, the administrator may challenge that order.

issues.legal_issue: Claims to exclude property from evacuee-property status cannot be newly entertained after the applicable outer limit, and pending stale claims are subject to dismissal, while finally adjudicated claims are not reopened on that basis.
material_facts: The governing provision required a claim to be made within thirty days of the relevant notification or demand but allowed delayed applications for sufficient recorded reasons.
The Court held that the extension could not permit a claim beyond twelve years from the property’s vesting in the Custodian.
The claimant’s predecessor applied within twelve years, and no limitation objection had been raised against that claim before the Court considered the issue.
The Court directed that new applications not be entertained, that pending applications entertained after twelve years be dismissed, and that claims already finally decided not be reopened.
issues.conclusion: The Court established the twelve-year outer limit and its prospective and pending-case consequences, but declined to reject this claimant’s claim as time-barred because it had been filed within that limit and limitation had not previously been raised.
issues.legal_principle: Section 8(2) made the stated filing period mandatory, subject to the Custodian’s power to allow delay for sufficient reasons recorded. That power did not authorize unlimited delay; the Court treated twelve years as the outer limit by reference to Section 28 and Article 142 of the Jammu and Kashmir Limitation Act. The Court held that the direction applied to pending, unadjudicated claims and did not reopen claims already finally adjudicated.

predicates.claim_to_exclude_property_from_protected: A person seeks to have property removed from the statutory administrator’s protected estate on the ground that it is not properly included in that estate or that the person’s interest was not affected.
predicates.new_claim_after_outer_limit: The person first seeks to bring the claim after the outer limit recognized by the Court has elapsed.
predicates.pending_claim_after_outer_limit: The claim was entertained after that outer limit and remains undecided.

issues.definition: A new claim brought after the outer limit cannot be entertained, and a still-pending claim entertained after that limit must be dismissed.

issues.legal_issue: Broad statutory revisional authority to examine the legality or propriety of an order may include consideration of factual findings.
material_facts: The Custodian General revised an order concerning restoration of the property and examined the evidence bearing on the claimant’s asserted interest and the effect of a will and probate.
The statute empowered the revisional authority to call for the record to examine the legality or propriety of an order and to make an order it considered fit.
The Custodian General found the evidence and asserted basis for restoration unreliable.
issues.conclusion: The Custodian General did not err by examining the facts in exercising the statutory revisional jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: The scope of revisional jurisdiction depends on the language of the statute conferring it. The power under Section 30(4) was wider than the limited revision power under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and permitted examination of factual matters relevant to legality and propriety. The Court relied on Rajbir Kaur & Anr. v. M/s S. Chokesiri & Co., Bhoolchand & Anr. v. Kay Pee Cee Investments & Anr., Ram Dass v. Ishwar Chander & Ors., Shiv Sarup Gupta v. Mahesh Chand Gupta, Mammu v. Hari Mohan & Anr., and Ram Narain Arora v. Asha Rani & Ors.

predicates.statutory_revision: A party or authority invokes a statutory process for reviewing an order of a subordinate authority.
predicates.revision_power_covers_legality_or_propri: The governing law authorizes the reviewing authority to examine the legality or propriety of the order and make an appropriate order.
predicates.facts_bear_on_legality_or_propriety: The facts under review are relevant to whether the challenged order was legally or properly made.

issues.definition: In statutory revision, an authority whose review power covers legality or propriety may examine facts relevant to those matters.

issues.legal_issue: A will and probate do not confer a right to property that the testator did not own or have authority to bequeath.
material_facts: The disputed property was vested in the Custodian when the will was executed.
The testator’s claim to the property had not been allowed; the application had been remanded and was later dismissed for non-appearance before her death.
The will did not establish that the testator owned the disputed property, and the probate proceedings did not determine title to that property.
issues.conclusion: Neither the will nor the probate conferred on the beneficiary a right to have the disputed property removed from the Custodian’s records or restored.
issues.legal_principle: Probate conclusively establishes the appointment of an executor and valid execution of a will, but it does not decide title to property mentioned in the will or establish that the testator owned it. A person cannot bequeath property in which the person had no right or interest. The Court relied on Smt. Rukmani Devi & Ors. v. Narendra Lal Gupta and Chiranjilal Shrilal Goenka v. Jasjit Singh & Ors. for the effect of probate, while distinguishing that effect from proof of title.

predicates.testator_did_not_own_property: The person who made the will had no established ownership or interest in the property when the will was made.
predicates.beneficiary_relies_on_will_or_probate: A beneficiary relies on the will or a grant of probate as the basis for claiming the property.

issues.definition: A beneficiary relying on a will or probate acquires no right to property that the testator did not own.

issues.legal_issue: A claim dismissed for non-appearance cannot be pursued as a fresh claim on the same facts and property without using the prescribed procedure to set aside the dismissal.
material_facts: The predecessor’s claim was dismissed for non-appearance.
The later applicant filed another application concerning the same property and facts, treating it as a continuation of the earlier claim.
The later applicant did not apply under the prescribed procedure to set aside the dismissal.
issues.conclusion: The later application was not a continuation of the dismissed claim, and the Custodian lacked jurisdiction to entertain it as a fresh application on the same facts and property.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 15(3) permitted dismissal for non-appearance. Rule 15(4) precluded a fresh application on the same facts concerning the same property, while allowing the applicant to seek setting aside of the dismissal within the prescribed period by showing sufficient cause.

predicates.claim_dismissed_for_nonappearance: An earlier claim concerning the property was dismissed because the applicant failed to appear when the matter was called.
predicates.later_claim_repeats_same_facts_and_prope: A later application seeks relief concerning the same property on the same factual basis as the dismissed claim.
predicates.setting_aside_request_not_timely_made: The applicant did not seek, within the permitted period, to have the dismissal set aside by showing sufficient cause.

issues.definition: A repeated claim on the same facts and property cannot be entertained as a fresh application when the earlier non-appearance dismissal was not timely set aside.

issues.legal_issue: Disputed title and succession questions cannot be determined as though they were ordinary claims under the statutory property-administration process.
material_facts: The claimant asserted a right through a will and a claimed family relationship, but the asserted interest and succession were disputed.
The claimant had not obtained a civil-court determination of his title or succession rights.
The statutory process provided for summary inquiry into claims, while the Court held that it did not authorize adjudication of disputed title or succession.
issues.conclusion: The statutory authorities could consider a claim based on undisputed admitted facts, but the disputed title and succession questions required proceedings in a civil court.
issues.legal_principle: The Act neither superseded the law of succession nor empowered its authorities to adjudicate disputed succession rights. An undisputed claim on admitted facts could be addressed under the Act’s procedure, but disputed questions of title had to be determined in appropriate civil proceedings.

predicates.statutory_property_claim: A person seeks relief concerning property through a statutory process for administering and protecting that property.
predicates.claimant_title_or_succession_is_disputed: The claimant’s asserted ownership, family relationship, or right of succession is contested and requires a determination of title.

issues.definition: When title or succession is disputed in a statutory property claim, the dispute must be determined in a civil court.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory claim to exclude property from evacuee status and the statutory claim to restore property to an evacuee address distinct situations and do not give a non-evacuee heir of an exclusion claimant a restoration right.
material_facts: The claimant’s predecessor sought exclusion of the property from the Custodian’s estate, while the later claimant relied on inheritance from that predecessor.
The predecessor’s claim had not resulted in her acquiring ownership before the will was made or before her death.
The restoration procedure applied to an evacuee or a person claiming as heir of the evacuee and required the specified governmental certification and supporting conditions.
The later claimant was not claiming as an evacuee who had returned, and was not shown to be an heir of the evacuee who owned the property.
issues.conclusion: The exclusion and restoration provisions applied to different contingencies, and no restoration right passed to the claimant merely by becoming heir to a person who had claimed exclusion.
issues.legal_principle: Section 8 concerns a claim that property is not evacuee property or that the claimant’s interest was not affected by the Act. Section 14 concerns restoration to an evacuee or the evacuee’s heir, subject to the statutory conditions. The Court held that an heir of a claimant under the exclusion provision does not thereby acquire a restoration right; a person who did not become an evacuee cannot claim on an evacuee’s behalf merely by becoming an heir with the passage of time.

rule.if: claimant_seeks_restoration_as_heir and predecessor_was_only_exclusion_claimant and claimant_is_not_ev evacuee_or_heir_of_ev evacuee

predicates.claimant_seeks_restoration_as_heir: A person seeks restoration of protected property on the basis of inheritance from another claimant.
predicates.predecessor_was_only_exclusion_claimant: The predecessor sought to establish that the property should not have been included in the protected estate but had not established ownership of it.
predicates.claimant_is_not_ev evacuee_or_heir_of_ev: The claimant is neither an evacuee seeking restoration nor an heir of the evacuee who owned the property.

issues.definition: A person who is neither the relevant evacuee nor that evacuee’s heir cannot obtain a restoration right solely through a predecessor who had made an exclusion claim.

issues.legal_issue: Occupants whose possession may be affected by a claim to evacuee property are necessary participants in proceedings deciding that claim.
material_facts: Tenants held the disputed property under allotments made by the Custodian.
An order allowing the restoration claim could affect the tenants’ possession.
The applicable procedure contemplated notice to interested persons, and the tenants had an interest in the property while occupying it.
issues.conclusion: The occupants were necessary parties and had to be given notice before a claim concerning restoration or exclusion of the property was adjudicated.
issues.legal_principle: A necessary party is one without whom an effective order cannot be made; a proper party is one whose presence is needed for a complete and final decision. The Court relied on Udit Narain Singh Malpaharia v. Additional Member Board of Revenue, Bihar & Anr., and held that occupants with legally protected possession must be notified in proceedings under the property-claim and restoration procedures.

predicates.occupant_has_protected_possession: A person occupies the property under a statutory allotment or other legally protected arrangement.
predicates.claim_order_may_affect_possession: The decision on another person’s property claim could affect the occupant’s continued possession.

issues.definition: An occupant with protected possession must be joined or notified when the property claim could affect that possession.
